An SCSA is defined as including two or more contiguous SMSA's which meet specified criteria of size and integration. To date, SCSA's have been defined for 13 metropolitan areas in which the characteristics of development and integration associated with SMSA's have been found to be displayed on a wide geographic scale.
There are a number of factors to keep in mind when considering adoption of SMSA's and SCSA's to define commercial and terminal zone areas:
1) The SMSA, by definition, includes the entire county and contiguous counties of population centers. While this would greatly simplify the method of identifying a given commercial zone, in certain instances, a substantial area that is not economically a part of the population center would nevertheless be included in a commercial zone. An outstanding example of this outcome is the Duluth-Superior SMSA which includes the entirety of St. Louis County, Minn. which extends over one hundred miles to the Canadian border.
2) SMSA's are continuously being updated on the basis of decennial census data, and consequently are an up-to-date representation of economic integration,
3) In many regions there are no SMSA's established. Consequently, resort to an alternative method of determining the commercial zone, such as a modified population-mileage formula, would be required.
The environmental impacts associated with this alternative are of the same nature as those previously discussed for the proposed population-mileage formula. However, this would effectively exempt motor carrier operations from economic regulation over a greatly expanded and broad geographic region. In addition, as a commercial zone expands away from the central city (into areas with reduced population and commercial densities) the beneficial environmental impacts potentially available through reduced central city VMT and congestion are less evident.
Executive Office of the President, Bureau of the Budget, Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas, 1967.
